reading.body:
Illinois has 376 AI-related bills in this dataset, and almost all of them are still just introduced.

The pattern is volume without enactment. Of the 376 bills, a large majority carry Introduced status, a smaller group reached Engrossed, and only a handful passed. The passed bills that touch AI directly are narrow: teacher evaluation, community college instructors, digital replicas. The broad framework bills, AI safety measures, chatbot liability, algorithmic pricing disclosure, AI product liability, sit at Introduced. The subject matter splits into two clusters. One is AI as a consumer and civil rights problem: pricing, hiring, health insurance, deepfakes, data privacy. The other is AI as physical infrastructure: data centers, hyperscale data centers, data center property rights, foreign ownership of data centers, data center heating and cooling, municipal referendums on data centers, and a resolution urging data centers to supply their own energy. That second cluster is where the compute and power story lives, and it is the more concrete of the two.

For AI specifically, the infrastructure bills matter more than the safety bills right now. A bill on hyperscale data centers or data center foreign ownership changes where compute can be built and who can own it. A bill on AI safety that never leaves committee changes nothing. The dataset shows a state generating a lot of legislative language about AI and very little binding law about it, while the bills that would shape the physical footprint of compute are moving through the same slow process.

What this does not tell you: whether any Introduced bill will pass, what the bills actually say, or how they compare to other states. It also does not include court cases, agency rules, or local ordinances, despite the page being framed around lawsuits. The four news items are a mix, and only one is clearly about Illinois AI law. Read the counts as activity, not outcomes.
